title: Urban foxes, pigeons and what counts as wildlife

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: There's a petition to cull the foxes on the estate and another one to leave them alone. Same estate, same week.

turns.speaker: Suri
turns.text: Culling urban foxes doesn't work anyway, which is the part that settles it practically.

turns.speaker: Blair
turns.text: Because the territory just gets filled.

turns.speaker: Suri
turns.text: Within weeks. Remove a family and neighbouring foxes expand into the gap, so you get the same density and more fighting.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: So the only thing that changes density is food.

turns.speaker: Suri
turns.text: Bins, mostly. A city with secured waste has fewer foxes without anyone doing anything else.

turns.speaker: Blair
turns.text: The pigeon situation is the same argument and people find it less charming.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Pigeons get treated as vermin and foxes get treated as wildlife, and the only real difference is that one of them is attractive.

turns.speaker: Suri
turns.text: Which is worth noticing, because conservation funding works the same way. Large mammals get money and invertebrates don't.

turns.speaker: Blair
turns.text: Although a fox in a garden at night is genuinely different from a fox on a nature documentary.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: That's fair. Proximity changes how people feel about anything.

turns.speaker: Suri
turns.text: The honest position is that these animals are adapted to us rather than surviving despite us.

turns.speaker: Blair
turns.text: Which makes them a consequence of how we live rather than an invasion of it.

points: Competing petitions call for culling and protecting urban foxes.
Suri argues culling fails because neighbouring foxes fill vacated territory within weeks, restoring density and increasing conflict.
Food availability, chiefly waste, is the only effective control on population.
Tom notes pigeons are treated as vermin and foxes as wildlife largely because of appearance.
Suri extends this to conservation funding, which favours large mammals over invertebrates.
They conclude urban animals are adapted to human habits rather than surviving despite them, making them a consequence of how cities operate.
